topics.title: Saheb of Seemapuri: garbage and wonder

learn.hook: Every morning, before most of Delhi wakes, children with sacks on their shoulders are already searching through the city's garbage. Anees Jung asks them why.
points: Author: Anees Jung, an Indian journalist and writer. The chapter is an extract from her book 'Lost Spring: Stories of Stolen Childhood'.
Form: a two-part reportage on child labour and poverty: Part 1 on Saheb, a ragpicker in Delhi; Part 2 on Mukesh, a bangle-maker's son in Firozabad.
Saheb-e-Alam's family came from Dhaka, Bangladesh, after storms swept away their fields and homes.
They live in Seemapuri, on the outskirts of Delhi, in mud structures with roofs of tin and tarpaulin, without sewage, drainage or running water.
For the elders ragpicking is a means of survival; for the children garbage is wrapped in wonder, because they may find a coin or even a ten-rupee note.

example.q: Why does the author say garbage means different things to children and to elders?
steps: Elders depend on what they collect to feed the family: survival.
Children are thrilled by the chance of finding a coin: wonder.
So the same garbage is a hard job for one and a treasure hunt for the other.
example.answer: For elders it is a means of survival; for children it holds the wonder of a possible find, like a coin.

learn.reallife: India's National Child Labour Project and the Right to Education Act (free schooling for ages 6–14) aim to move children like Saheb from rag sacks to school bags.

topics.title: Barefoot, a grand name and a lost freedom

learn.hook: A boy named 'Lord of the Universe' cannot afford a pair of chappals. Anees Jung lets that irony speak for itself.
points: Many children walk barefoot. Some say it is a tradition, but the author suspects this explains away constant poverty.
Saheb-e-Alam means 'lord of the universe', ironic for a barefoot boy who picks rags.
The author jokingly asks if he would go to school if she started one; days later he asks if her school is ready, and she feels embarrassed by her empty promise.
Later Saheb works at a tea stall for 800 rupees and all his meals. He now carries a steel canister instead of his plastic bag.
He has lost his freedom: the bag was his, but the canister belongs to the tea-stall owner. He is no longer his own master.

example.q: Is Saheb happier at the tea stall? Explain.
steps: He earns 800 rupees and gets meals, so he is better fed.
But his carefree look is gone; the steel canister feels heavier than the bag.
The bag was his own; now he works for a master.
example.answer: No. He earns more, but he has lost his freedom and carefree spirit; he is no longer his own master.

learn.reallife: Thousands of children still work at dhabas and tea stalls in India. Their wages may seem like progress, but the cost is their childhood and schooling.

learn.hook: Bright glass bangles jingle at weddings across India. Few buyers think of the dark rooms where they are made.
points: Mukesh lives in Firozabad, the centre of India's glass-bangle industry.
About 20,000 children work near high-temperature furnaces and glass-blowing units in dingy cells without air and light; many lose their eyesight before they become adults.
Child labour is illegal, yet it thrives; families have made bangles for generations.
Savita, a young girl in a drab pink dress, solders pieces of glass beside an elderly woman.
Bangles symbolise a married Indian woman's auspiciousness (suhaag); Savita may not yet know the sanctity of what she is making.

example.q: Why is there irony in Savita making bangles?
steps: Bangles are a symbol of a married woman's good fortune.
Savita is a young girl working in grim conditions, not enjoying any such fortune.
She makes symbols of joy while her own childhood is lost.
example.answer: She makes the symbols of a happy married life while her own life is joyless labour.

learn.reallife: Studies of the Firozabad glass industry have long reported eye and lung problems among workers. Safety rules and bans on child labour exist, but enforcement is the real challenge.

topics.title: The vicious circle and Mukesh's dream

learn.hook: Imagine making something beautiful all your life and never once eating a full meal. An old bangle maker lives that truth.
points: An elderly woman says she has not enjoyed even one full meal in her whole life, though she has made bangles throughout it.
The workers are trapped in a vicious circle of sahukars (moneylenders), middlemen, policemen, keepers of the law, bureaucrats and politicians.
They cannot organise: if they did, they fear being hauled up by the police, beaten and jailed; there is no leader and no cooperative.
Mukesh is different. He dreams of being a motor mechanic and driving a car, a dream that breaks away from the family tradition of bangle making.

example.q: Why does the author see Mukesh's dream as hopeful?
steps: Everyone around him accepts bangle making as destiny.
Mukesh wants to be a motor mechanic and learn to drive a car.
Choosing his own path shows courage to break the circle.
example.answer: His dream to be a motor mechanic breaks away from the inherited trade, showing courage and hope.

learn.reallife: Self-help groups and cooperatives, like those under India's DAY-NRLM mission, help artisans sell without middlemen. That is exactly what the bangle workers lacked.

topics.title: Themes, the title, and answer writing

learn.hook: Spring is the season of new leaves. Childhood is the spring of life. What happens when a child never gets one?
points: Child labour and the loss of childhood: children like Saheb and Savita work instead of playing and learning.
Poverty and exploitation, made worse by the burden of tradition and fate (karam), which people accept without question.
Hope: Mukesh's dream and Saheb's interest in school show that the wish for a better life survives.
Title metaphor: 'spring' stands for childhood; 'lost spring' means childhood stolen by poverty and work.
Answer writing: short answers (40–50 words) on Saheb or Mukesh need one key point plus a detail; a long answer on child labour should cover causes, effects and solutions.

example.q: Explain the title 'Lost Spring' in about 40 words.
steps: Saheb and Mukesh lose this stage to labour and poverty.
example.answer: Spring symbolises childhood. Saheb and Mukesh lose the joys of childhood, like play and school, to poverty and labour, so the title means 'stolen childhood'.

learn.reallife: India's 2011 Census counted about one crore working children aged 5–14. Every one of those numbers is a 'lost spring'.

topics.title: Craft and questions: reportage, irony, and the role of society

learn.hook: A news report gives numbers. A reportage like this gives names, faces and voices, and that is why you remember it.
points: Reportage technique: first-hand observation, real names, dialogue ('Is your school ready?') and vivid imagery.
Irony: Saheb's grand name against his poverty; bright, colourful bangles against the grim lives of their makers.

Think-as-you-read answers: Saheb looks for coins in garbage; he lives in Seemapuri because storms drove his family from Dhaka; children go barefoot because of poverty; Saheb is not happy at the tea stall because he has lost his freedom.
Understanding the text: Mukesh dreams of being a motor mechanic; the bangle industry harms eyesight; workers cannot organise for fear of the police and lack of a cooperative.
Society's role: enforce child-labour laws, provide schools, form cooperatives and spread awareness among buyers.

example.q: How does the author make the reader feel Saheb's reality, not just know about it?
steps: She uses his real name and its meaning.
She quotes his words and her own.
She describes Seemapuri in concrete detail: mud, tin, tarpaulin.
example.answer: Through real names, dialogue and vivid concrete detail, typical of reportage.

learn.reallife: Campaigns like Bachpan Bachao Andolan, founded by Nobel laureate Kailash Satyarthi, rescue child workers. Public pressure is part of society's role.
